clue.text: Fax from CID line scuppered publicist

indicators.note: a scuppered ship is wrecked, so the letters before it are broken up and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A fax from the police has sunk some spin doctor's plans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scuppered' rearranges FAXFROMCID plus L for line. Max Clifford was the best-known British tabloid publicist of the 1990s.
explanation.definitionFit: Max Clifford was a celebrated PR agent who sold kiss-and-tell stories to the tabloids.

clue.text: Note to 'Sir' torn up the story of your life?

parts.note: a memo is a short note

indicators.note: something torn up is ripped to pieces, so the letters of Sir are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone ripping up a note addressed to a knight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'torn up' looks like a down-clue reversal, but reversing would give RIS; tearing up scrambles the title into IRS instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Memoirs are a written account of one's own life.

clue.text: Someone who's against outsiders vandalising phone boxes pointlessly

indicators.note: vandalising means smashing up, so the letters are rearranged
pointlessly means without a compass point, so one S for south is dropped

explanation.surface: A bigot smashing up telephone boxes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pointlessly' takes S, a compass point, from PHONEBOXES to leave PHONEBOXE, and 'vandalising' rearranges that.
explanation.definitionFit: A xenophobe fears or dislikes foreigners.

clue.text: Whoppers are to be found on a Pole

parts.note: to lie somewhere is to be found there
S is the South Pole, one of the poles

explanation.surface: Big lies told about a Polish person.
explanation.walkthrough: Pole looks like a Polish person; the capital hides the South Pole.
explanation.definitionFit: Whoppers are blatant untruths.

clue.text: Tawdry queen, one who outs member

parts.note: flash means showy and cheap
ER is the cipher of Queen Elizabeth

explanation.surface: A cheap queen exposing another member's secret.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outs' and 'queen' suggest gay outing; the member is a body part exposed.
explanation.definitionFit: A flasher exposes his genitals in public, a crude sense of member.

clue.text: Some catastrophe liable to reveal Bill's character

indicators.note: some of the following words means only part of them gives the answer

parts.note: the letters run across the end of catastrophe and the start of liable

explanation.surface: A disaster that could expose a man's true nature.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill is William Shakespeare, so his character is someone in one of his plays.
explanation.definitionFit: Ophelia is the tragic heroine in Shakespeare's Hamlet.

clue.text: Bimbo fair gets mum light-headed

parts.note: mum means silent, as does dumb
fair-haired means blonde

explanation.surface: A pretty blonde making her mother dizzy.
explanation.walkthrough: Mum is not a mother here but silent, as in keeping mum.
explanation.definitionFit: A dumb blonde is the stereotype of an attractive but empty-headed woman, which a bimbo is.

clue.text: The little woman needs good poke!

parts.note: Jo March is the heroine of Little Women, so one little woman is Jo

explanation.surface: A crude remark about a wife wanting a good poke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The little woman' looks like a husband's name for his wife, but it points to Jo of Little Women.
explanation.definitionFit: To jog someone is to nudge or prod them, a light poke.

clue.text: Judgmental type of royal biographer having change of heart

indicators.note: a change of heart swaps the middle letter of the name for another

parts.note: Penny Junor wrote biographies of Prince Charles and Diana

explanation.surface: A writer of royal lives turning critical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having change of heart' swaps the central N of JUNOR for R.
explanation.definitionFit: A juror sits on a jury and helps judge a case.

clue.text: Private Eye underground, subverted? Shome mistake?

indicators.note: subverted means turned upside down, so in a down clue the letters are read bottom up

parts.note: UG is an abbreviation for underground

indicators.note: a mistake gets things wrong, so the letters are muddled

explanation.surface: Private Eye's own catchphrase about a drunk's slurred error.
explanation.walkthrough: 'subverted' turns UG into GU and 'mistake' jumbles SHOME into MSHOE. 'Shome mistake shurely' is a Private Eye catchphrase; the clue's Private Eye is the detective.
explanation.definitionFit: A gumshoe is American slang for a detective.

clue.text: Nelson also into male buggery

indicators.note: into says the word for also is put inside the other letters
buggery is used loosely for messing something up, so the letters of male are jumbled

parts.note: also means and

explanation.surface: A scurrilous rumour linking a famous Nelson with a sex scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: Nelson suggests the admiral, but it is the South African leader; 'buggery' jumbles male into MELA and 'into' sends also inside after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Nelson Mandela, the South African president, is the famous bearer of this forename.

clue.text: Stink connected with rap is tiresome

parts.note: hum is British slang for a bad smell
to drum is to rap repeatedly with the fingers

explanation.surface: A grumble that rap music stinks and is boring.
explanation.walkthrough: Rap here is not music but a tapping sound; hum is everyday British slang for a smell.
explanation.definitionFit: Something humdrum is dull and monotonous, lacking any excitement.

clue.text: Trouble-makers backing Blair's intrusion into lives

indicators.note: an intrusion into something goes inside it, so the reversed piece sits within the word for lives

parts.note: lives means is, as in 'he is'

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the letters for Blair are read right to left

parts.note: Tony Blair was the PM, Prime Minister

explanation.surface: Critics complaining that Blair's government pries into private lives.
explanation.walkthrough: Blair stands for his office of Prime Minister; 'backing' flips that title to MP and 'intrusion into' pushes it inside the word for lives, as in 'he is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Imps are mischievous little devils, so trouble-makers in a small way.

clue.text: Labour's minor beginnings

definitions.note: read as 'Labour is', so the definition is the noun labour

parts.note: a minor is a child in law
a birth is the beginning of something

explanation.surface: A jibe at the Labour Party's modest origins.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital L makes Labour look like the political party; it is labour in the delivery-room sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Labour is the process of giving birth, so it equals childbirth.

clue.text: Say a drug-induced session withE '' is bollocks

parts.note: to utter is to say
a trip is a spell under a hallucinogen
the source runs with and E together; E stands for Ecstasy, the letter itself

explanation.surface: Dismissing a drug-fuelled night out as rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: The source prints 'withE' with a stray quote mark; the clue reads 'with E'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bollocks is British slang for nonsense, which utter tripe also means.

clue.text: No place on Blue Peter for such a horsey-sounding type?

definitions.text: No place on Blue Peter for such a horsey-sounding type?

parts.words: No place on Blue Peter for such a horsey-sounding type?
parts.note: Blue Peter sacked a presenter in 1998 for taking cocaine, and horses make a nasal blowing noise

explanation.surface: A jokey question about who the children's show should not hire.
explanation.walkthrough: Blue Peter is a long-running BBC children's programme; presenter Richard Bacon was sacked in 1998 after a cocaine story. A snorter takes cocaine up the nose, and snorting is also a horse's noise.
explanation.definitionFit: A snorter is someone who sniffs cocaine, and the word also suits a horse blowing through its nostrils.

clue.text: Peter possibly bitter about Mail

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the drink goes round the letters for mail

parts.note: bitter is a British beer, an ale
post means mail, letters delivered

explanation.surface: Someone called Peter is cross about the Daily Mail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps the beer round the letters. The capital M makes Mail look like the Daily Mail newspaper; bitter is a British beer, and Peter is the saint, not Mandelson.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Peter was one of the twelve disciples of Jesus, an example of the type.

clue.text: Getting an erection makes belly whiff, note, internally

indicators.note: internally means the note goes inside the other pieces

parts.note: tum is a colloquial word for belly
a whiff is a smell, a scent
E is a musical note

explanation.surface: A crude remark about a smell and arousal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'internally' puts the musical note in the middle of the belly-and-whiff pair; tum is British nursery talk for stomach.
explanation.definitionFit: Tumescent means swollen, as an aroused penis becomes.

clue.text: Main barriers around Brenda's joints

indicators.note: around means the barriers enclose the royal letters

parts.note: reefs are barriers in the main, the open sea
Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, whose cipher is ER

explanation.surface: Sea defences built round the Queen's limbs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' wraps the barriers round the royal cipher. Private Eye calls the Queen Brenda; main is the old word for the sea, and joints are cannabis cigarettes, not knees.
explanation.definitionFit: Reefers are hand-rolled cannabis cigarettes, also called joints.

clue.text: Of high standing in California, but not with British voters?

definitions.text: Of high standing in California, but not with British voters?

parts.words: Of high standing in California, but not with British voters?
parts.note: California's giant trees stand tall, while the Tory politician of that name was unpopular with British voters

explanation.walkthrough: John Redwood was a right-wing Conservative minister who challenged John Major in 1995; the tree is the tall Californian sequoia.
explanation.definitionFit: The redwood is a towering conifer of California; the surname belonged to an unpopular Tory politician.

clue.text: Smack right for a footballer?

parts.note: to strike is to hit, smack

explanation.surface: Hitting a footballer on the right.
explanation.walkthrough: Smack might suggest heroin; it is a blow.
explanation.definitionFit: A striker is a forward whose job is to score goals.

clue.text: Native to offer Ecstasy to bent CID men

parts.note: E is the street abbreviation for the drug Ecstasy

indicators.note: bent means twisted, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Bribing corrupt detectives with Ecstasy pills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bent' reads as corrupt police; it is the signal to rearrange E plus CIDMEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Something endemic is native to or found regularly in a particular place.

clue.text: Smashed, so tried to be hacks

indicators.note: smashed means broken up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Drunk journalists trying to be reporters.
explanation.walkthrough: Smashed looks like drunk, the natural reading for hacks.
explanation.definitionFit: Hack is a slang term for a journalist; editors are senior ones.

clue.text: This crossword is Cyclops's first reverse — pity about copyright

indicators.note: first means only the opening letter of the setter's name is used

parts.note: Cyclops is the setter, and only his opening letter is used
R is the gear-stick marking for reverse

indicators.note: about means turned around and rearranged, so the letters of pity are mixed

parts.note: C is the copyright symbol

explanation.surface: Cyclops regretting a copyright problem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' takes C from Cyclops; R marks reverse on a gearstick; 'about' mixes PITY into YPTI; C in a circle is the copyright mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic crossword uses puzzling wordplay clues, as Private Eye's does.

clue.text: Mounted, he pinched penis, roughly put in about right

parts.note: dick is slang for penis

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the rearranged letters go round the letter for right
roughly means approximately arranged, so the letters of put in are jumbled

explanation.surface: A lurid account of a sexual assault by a man on horseback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roughly' rearranges PUT IN into TUPIN, and 'about' puts it round R. Dick Turpin was the famous 18th-century English highwayman.
explanation.definitionFit: Dick Turpin was a highwayman who robbed travellers on horseback, a mounted thief.

clue.text: Scrounge from arsehole, obtain time off

parts.note: a cad is a dishonourable man, a rotter

indicators.note: off means taken away, so the letter for time is dropped

parts.note: to get is to obtain

explanation.surface: Getting money from some rotter, taking time off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' drops T from GET to leave GE. Arsehole is British slang for an unpleasant man, as cad is.
explanation.definitionFit: To cadge is to beg or borrow without intending to repay.

clue.text: Take our mag, we hear, and make out it's child's play!

indicators.note: we hear means the word is taken by its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: the magazine is Private Eye, so our mag is Eye
to spy is to make out or catch sight of

explanation.surface: An advert telling readers to buy the magazine and enjoy it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear' turns EYE, short for Private Eye, into the letter I by sound.
explanation.definitionFit: I spy is a guessing game for children played by naming things seen.

clue.text: "Public toilets extremely lacking" — TV reporter

indicators.note: lacking its extremes means without first and last letters

parts.note: Ladies is a British sign for women's public toilets

explanation.surface: A news report that the public toilets are inadequate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely lacking' drops the outer letters of LADIES. Kate Adie was the BBC's chief news correspondent, famous for war zones.
explanation.definitionFit: Kate Adie was a well-known BBC television reporter.

clue.text: Past its sell-by date can? The devil it is!

parts.note: something past its sell-by date is old
can is slang for prison, as is the British nick

explanation.surface: Finding an out-of-date tin and cursing it.
explanation.walkthrough: Can looks like a tin, but it means prison, which in Britain is also the nick.
explanation.definitionFit: Old Nick is a traditional nickname for Satan.

clue.text: Queer blokes having time for a bit

parts.note: queer in its old sense means odd
blokes are men

explanation.surface: Gay men passing the time with each other for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: Queer is in its old sense of strange.
explanation.definitionFit: An oddment is a leftover scrap or piece of something.

clue.text: Take on a different hue, as embraced by Mandy, evidently

indicators.note: embraced by means held inside, so the letters sit within the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of Mandy and the start of evidently

explanation.surface: Peter Mandelson, nicknamed Mandy, apparently changing colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'embraced by' says the letters sit within 'Mandy, evidently'. Mandy was Private Eye's name for Peter Mandelson.
explanation.definitionFit: To dye something is to change its colour.

clue.text: Awfully precious, etc like many a Conservative party member?

definitions.text: like many a Conservative party member

indicators.note: awfully means badly done, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A sneer at the precious, fussy members of the Tory party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awfully' reads as 'very' modifying precious, but it is the signal to rearrange PRECIOUS and ETC.
explanation.definitionFit: Many Tories were hostile to the European Union, so sceptical about Europe.
